payload.source_label: The quasilinear form suggests hyperbolicity when the flux Jacobian satisfies the matrix condition

contract.statement: For the one-dimensional conservation law q_t + (f(q))_x = 0, the quasilinear form is q_t + f′(q)q_x = 0. The source says the equation is hyperbolic if the flux Jacobian satisfies the earlier condition for a constant real coefficient matrix: real eigenvalues together with m corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors forming a basis of R^m [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening paragraph and equations (1.8)–(1.9) with the following sentence; real-state setting on raw PDF page 23, printed page 1]. The passage does not require distinct eigenvalues, specify the state domain over which the condition must hold, or prescribe a precise differentiability class. Its differential interpretation carries smoothness qualifications acknowledged in the discussion of discontinuous solutions [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, Section 1.1.2].
assumptions: The equation under discussion is the one-dimensional homogeneous conservation law q_t + (f(q))_x = 0, written in quasilinear form q_t + f′(q)q_x = 0 [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, equations (1.8)–(1.9)].

The flux Jacobian f′(q) has real eigenvalues and m linearly independent corresponding eigenvectors, with the real-space interpretation supported by the stated decomposition of every vector in R^m [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening paragraph and sentence after equation (1.9)].

Existence of the derivatives and applicability of the chain rule are implicit in the displayed quasilinear rewriting; no precise differentiability class is stated there [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, 'Rewriting this in the quasilinear form' and equation (1.9)].

The selected passage concerns first-order systems in one spatial dimension; the source explicitly restricts the book's discussion to first-order hyperbolic systems [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, introduction to equation (1.1); raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, paragraph following equation (1.7)].

The pointwise spectral criterion is inherited from a constant real matrix, but f′(q) may vary with q because nonlinear fluxes are allowed [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, equation (1.9); raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, opening paragraph].

The differential and quasilinear expressions belong to a smooth setting. The source separately warns that conservation-law solutions can be discontinuous and qualifies derivation of the differential form from the integral form by sufficient smoothness [raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, Section 1.1.2, opening paragraph].
quantifiers: Inherited setting: x and t are real spatial and temporal variables, and q : R × R → R^m is the vector-valued unknown; m counts its components [raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, equation (1.1) and following paragraph].

The flux f acts on the state q, and f′(q) is its m × m flux Jacobian; a flux between real m-dimensional state spaces is inherited from the system's dimensions, although no state-domain set is specified [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, equations (1.8)–(1.9); raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, definition of q and A].

At a state where the criterion is applied, there must exist m corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors with real eigenvalues. Indexing these pairs by i = 1, …, m is analyst notation for the source's 'set of m' [raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening hyperbolicity criterion and sentence after equation (1.9)].
